# History

Topics in this knowledge base concerning the history of China — its dynasties, eras, and the developments that shaped the nation from antiquity to the present.

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED: category-index — maintained by build-structure; do not edit by hand -->
| Topic | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| [The Xia Dynasty](the-xia-dynasty.md) | China's legendary first dynasty (c. 2070–1600 BCE), remembered as the bridge between myth and history; founded by Yu the Great after his taming of the Yellow River floods and ended by the tyrant Jie, it established the model of hereditary rule and Mandate-based legitimacy, and is tentatively linked by many scholars to the Bronze Age Erlitou culture. |
| [The Shang Dynasty](the-shang-dynasty.md) | China's earliest archaeologically and textually confirmed dynasty (c. 1600–1046 BCE) and the apex of its Bronze Age; it produced the oracle-bone script ancestral to modern Chinese writing, monumental ritual bronzes, a theocratic ancestor cult, and the scribal statecraft later dynasties inherited, before falling to the Zhou at the Battle of Muye. |
| [The Zhou Dynasty](the-zhou-dynasty.md) | China's longest-lasting dynasty (1046–256 BCE); it introduced the Mandate of Heaven, ruled through a *fengjian* network of vassal states, and—amid the fragmentation of its Spring and Autumn and Warring States eras—gave rise to Confucianism, Daoism, and the Hundred Schools of Thought before Qin's unification. |
| [The Warring States Period](warring-states-period.md) | An era of intense interstate conflict (475–221 BCE) when pre-imperial China fragmented into seven contending kingdoms; it produced mass infantry warfare, *The Art of War*, the "Hundred Schools of Thought," and Shang Yang's Legalist reforms before Qin's unification ended more than two centuries of division. |
| [The Qin Dynasty](the-qin-dynasty.md) | China's first centralized empire (221–206 BCE); unified the warring states, standardized writing, weights, measures, and currency, and created the bureaucratic imperial model that endured for over two millennia. |
| [The Han Dynasty](the-han-dynasty.md) | The second imperial dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE); made Confucianism the state ideology, opened the Silk Road under Emperor Wu, and set the template of centralized, meritocratic imperial rule that later dynasties emulated—so foundational that the Chinese majority is still called "Han." |
| [The Sui Dynasty](the-sui-dynasty.md) | A short-lived but pivotal dynasty (581–618 CE); reunified China after nearly three centuries of division, built the Grand Canal, and codified the Three Departments and Six Ministries and the examination system the Tang would inherit, before Emperor Yang's ruinous Goguryeo campaigns brought its collapse. |
| [The Tang Dynasty](the-tang-dynasty.md) | A golden age of Chinese civilization (618–907 CE); cosmopolitan, prosperous, and militarily powerful, it perfected the civil examination system and produced a canonical flowering of poetry, painting, and Silk Road exchange. |
| [The Song Dynasty](the-song-dynasty.md) | A culturally and technologically brilliant era (960–1279), divided into Northern (960–1127) and Southern (1127–1279) periods; it produced Neo-Confucianism, woodblock and movable-type printing, gunpowder weapons, the compass, and the world's first paper money before falling to the Mongols. |
| [The Yuan Dynasty](the-yuan-dynasty.md) | The Mongol empire's direct rule over China (1271–1368), established by Kublai Khan with its capital at Dadu (Beijing); a four-tier social hierarchy and dual administration accompanied a flowering of Yuan drama and unprecedented Eurasian trade under the *Pax Mongolica*, before floods, plague, and the Red Turban Rebellion brought the Ming restoration. |
| [The Ming Dynasty](the-ming-dynasty.md) | A powerful, culturally prolific Han-Chinese dynasty (1368–1644 CE); built the Forbidden City and the iconic Great Wall, sponsored Zheng He's maritime voyages, then turned inward before falling to the Qing. |
| [The Qing Dynasty](the-qing-dynasty.md) | The last imperial dynasty (1644–1912 CE), established by the Manchus; expanded China to its greatest territorial extent and presided over a cultural golden age, but proved unable to withstand Western and Japanese pressure, collapsing in the 1911 Xinhai Revolution. |
| [The Opium Wars](the-opium-wars.md) | Two mid-19th-century conflicts (1839–1842 and 1856–1860) in which Britain, later joined by France, forced the Qing to open its markets, cede Hong Kong, and accept the "unequal treaty system"—the opening blows of China's "Century of Humiliation." |
| [The Boxer Rebellion](the-boxer-rebellion.md) | A violent anti-foreign, anti-Christian uprising (1899–1901) in northern China; embraced by the late Qing court, its 55-day siege of Beijing's Legation Quarter drew an eight-nation military intervention whose punitive Boxer Protocol deepened the "Century of Humiliation" and hastened the dynasty's fall. |
| [The Long March](the-long-march.md) | The Communist Party's 1934–1935 military retreat of roughly 9,000 km from the Jiangxi Soviet to Yan'an; only a fraction of the 86,000 who set out survived, but Mao Zedong rose to pre-eminence at the Zunyi Conference and the party's core endured to win the Civil War. |
| [The Great Leap Forward](the-great-leap-forward.md) | Mao Zedong's 1958–1962 campaign to industrialize China through people's communes and backyard steel furnaces; its inflated targets and requisitions triggered history's deadliest famine, killing an estimated 30 million and discrediting Maoist economics. |
| [Cultural Revolution](cultural-revolution.md) | A decade of social and political upheaval (1966–1976) launched by Mao Zedong to purge perceived capitalist and traditional elements; Red Guard mobilization, mass persecution, and factional violence killed hundreds of thousands and left trauma central to modern China's self-understanding. |
